2. Appellant's father Amrita Lal Biswas and another, Shailendra Lal Dey, filed the suit being Title Suit No. 468 of 1957 in the Third Court of Munsif, Barisal which was, on transfer to the 6th Court of Munsif, Barisal, renumbered as Title Suit No. 71 of 1961, against the respondents-defendants for establishment of their auction-purchased right and title in the suit land, for confirmation of possession in the alternative for recovery of possession from the main defendants and also for an injunction against them. The Suit land measuring 1.99 acres and comprised in C.S. Khatian No. 797 of Monza Mahisha Gagaria originally belonged to three Pal brothers namely, Baikunta Pal, Puma Chandra Pal and Kailash Chandra Pal in Kaisha right under the superior landlords Kederesaban and others. The Karsha was put to sale for arrears of rent in connection with Rent Execution Case No. 432 of 1948 and the plaintiffs purchased the suit land in auction on February 19, 1949 and took delivery of possession through Court on July 14, 1949. Case of the plaintiffs is that after about a year i.e. in April May, 1950 they cams to know that one Basanta Dey and one Surendra Dey, predecessors of defendant Nos. 9 to 12 had, by fraudulent means, obtained lease of the land in Kol-karsha, right from Jalada Sundari, widow and heir of Baikunta, one of the three Pal brothers. The lease-deed, if any, creating the Kol-karsha, was never acted upon and the lessees never possessed the land, but the defendants claiming Kol-karsha right threatened to dispossess them from the land in 1954, and hence they filed the suit. 

 6. Mr. M.H. Khandakar, learned Counsel for the appellant has concentrated all his efforts on one point which is that under section 48F, Bengal Tenancy Act, an under-raiyati interest not being transferable without landlord's consent, transfer of the Kol-karsha to the defendants without landlord's consent amounted to abandonment of the holding by the under-raiyat whereupon the landlords, namely, the plaintiffs, got right of re-entry upon the land and to evict the transferee-defendants as mere trespassers. As to the question whether .the plaintiffs, on purchase of the karsha, annulled the Kol-karsha as encumbrance, Mr. Khondaker's contention is that a Kol-karsha was not an encumbrance within the meaning of section 161 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and as such it need not be annulled by the landlord under section 167, B.T. Act. In support of these contentions Mr. Khandaker has, of course, referred to a great number of decisions; but before we consider the principle of law formulated in those decisions we propose to look into the relevant facts of the case as on record in order to see the inconsistent stand taken by the plaintiff at the crucial turn of events in respect of the very existence of the defendants Kol-karsha created as far back as in 1938 under a registered Dakhila (Ext. B). At first the plaintiffs denied the existence of the Kol-karsha, They in their plaint stated that they purchased the suit land on 19.2.49 and took delivery of possession on 14.7.49 and since then they continued to be in possession till 1954 when, for the first time, the defendants threatened to dispossess them on the strength of a Kol-karsha right created by fraud and collusion whereas there was no Kol-karsha at all. If these were so, the question of annulment of any Kol-karsha, on plaintiffs' purchase of the karsha in Rent Execution case No. 32 of 1942, did not arise. But when the defendants led unchallengeable evidence, both oral and documentary, showing the creation of the Kol-karsha under Ext. B by Jalada Sundari, one of the owners in possession of the Karsha in favour of Basanta Kumer Dey, the recording of the defendants names in R. S. Khatians, and confirmation of the Kol-karsha in their case under section 174 (3) B. T. Act in which the Kol-karsha was found to have been in existence since 1938, the plaintiffs turned round and invoked section 48F, B.T. Act which provides that an under raiyati interest is not transferable without landlord's consent. This subsequent stand taken by the plaintiffs unerringly shows that they were aware of the existence of the Kol-karsha when they purchased the holding in 1949, but having failed to .go into actual possession of the land, took resort to falsehood by denying the existence of the Kol-korsha. They took delivery of possession through Court on 14.7.49 in consequence of their purchase, but the possession was clearly symbolical possession of the superior karsha right under which the Kol-karsha continued to exist undisturbed.
